newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FOCUS-Wienerberger posts limp earnings for 1996.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Wienerberger posts limp earnings for 1996.

text.p: Wienerberger Baustoffindustrie, the world's top brick maker, reported limp 1996 earnings on Tuesday but promised rosier returns this year as the European building materials industry lifts itself from the doldrums.
Wienerberger said net profit fell to 800 million schillings ($66.7 million) from 1.12 billion a year earlier, while pretax earnings eased to 1.37 billion schillings from 1.495 billion.
Earnings before taxes and interest (EBIT) fell to 1.60 billion schillings from 1.67 billion a year earlier. Group sales rose to 15.061 billion from 12.855 billion in 1995.
"1996 was a very difficult year for the European building materials industry," Wienerberger said in a statement.
It said austerity measures in both Germany and Austria, exacerbated by an unusually long and severe winter, had put a tight lid on prices and caused soaring excess capacities.
The group left its 1996 dividend unchanged at 42 schillings per share. Earnings per share fell to 104 schillings from 168 schillings a year ago, the Association of Austrian Analysts said.

The outlook for the current year was substantially better, Wienerberger said. After first-quarter pretax profit inched up to 36 million schillings from 30 million a year earlier, the group said it expected a 24 percent gain in full-year pretax earnings to around 1.7 billion schillings.

However, Wienerberger warned the first-quarter result had to be treated with some caution. "The first quarter is traditionally weak in the building materials industry and therefore little can be deduced from it," it said.

The group said the acquisition of Belgium's largest brick maker Terca Bricks last April had been a decisive factor in strengthening its earnings potential. "The acquisition of Terca has since proven to be a particularly great success," it said.
Terca contributed 2.374 billion schillings to sales and recorded a pretax profit of 341 million schillings.
At the same time, Wienerberger continued to consolidate its holdings in other parts of Europe.

While causing a charge of 200 million schillings against current-year earnings, the closure of six plants in Germany, Austria and Italy and the sale of two further plants had boosted capacity utilisation and cut production costs, it said.
Wienerberger, which is 32.2 percent controlled by Creditanstalt-Bankverein, now operates 157 plants in 21 countries on three continents.

The group's wall, ceiling and roofing systems unit, which accounts for almost half of total sales, provided the largest contribution to 1996 profits. However, without the acquisition of Terca, the unit would have seen a substantial drop in earnings, Wienerberger said without providing further detail.

Abrasive materials maker Treibacher, accounting for about 21 percent of turnover, saw sales slump by a quarter as prices and market conditions deteriorated. Still, Wienerberger said the unit showed "modest profits".

Investors took the results in their stride, marking Wienerberger's stock up nine schillings to 2,259 in midday trading in an otherwise limp Vienna market. "The figures were more or less in line with expectations," said a trader.
